source.title: Dual Dimensionality for Local and Global Attention
source.authors: Zhi-Yuan Wang; Xuan Luo; Si-Rui Zeng; Xi-Feng Yan

record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out perplexity under an attention-architecture change at fixed model scales, bearing on whether architecture details change loss only slightly (V4). It does not test the scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation in the other versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports pretraining perplexity for distance-adaptive and uniformly reduced attention representations, and reports downstream task scores. The downstream scores do not measure a version's stated loss or predictability relation, so they are not rows. The study does not fit or test power laws in model parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.test_reason: The window-size ablation tests V4 by changing attention routing while retaining the same bottleneck architecture and parameter shapes. DAR versus uniform reduction at the same bottleneck dimension also bears on V4. Comparisons against Vanilla do not establish fixed-parameter effects: DAR adds trainable down- and up-projections, and total parameter counts are not matched or reported.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that local and distant tokens have asymmetric representation requirements: moderate distant-token compression preserves pretraining perplexity and, after continued SFT, downstream performance, whereas uniform or sufficiently aggressive compression harms performance. Practical cache savings remain a proposed implementation direction.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains distance-adaptive attention representations and compares them with full-dimensional and uniform-reduction baselines; it does not fit scaling laws or estimate compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity varies with bottleneck dimension, uniform versus distance-adaptive reduction, and local window size.

fits_no_version.finding: DAR matches or improves Vanilla perplexity at nominal Pythia scales of 160M and 410M, but introduces additional trainable projections without matching total parameter counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distance-adaptive bottlenecks can preserve perplexity relative to their underlying full-dimensional model architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Continued SFT with moderate distant-token bottlenecks preserves downstream scores, while stronger compression reduces them; neither scale nor pretraining-loss predictability is evaluated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream capabilities tolerate moderate distance-adaptive representation compression after continued supervised fine-tuning.

record.problems: Pretraining coverage is limited to 70M–410M parameter models and one training-token budget of 10B; the paper says larger-scale and broader architecture evaluation remains future work. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 repeats the Pythia-70M DAR and Vanilla results already represented in Table 1, so those duplicates are not listed again. Table 4 downstream scores are not held-out pretraining loss or a test of downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Power-law loss dependence over several orders of magnitude in parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from fitted small runs to substantially larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations across compute budgets.
Depth and width sweeps, broader architecture families, and parameter-matched DAR-versus-Vanilla comparisons at different model scales.
Power-law forms outside ordinary text pretraining; the SFT experiment does not fit a scaling law.
Prediction of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Perplexity is exponential in cross-entropy loss, so percentage perplexity gaps should not be interpreted as equal percentage loss gaps. The scope-limiting contrasts establish sensitivity within this attention design, not a broad failure of scaling laws. No uncertainty estimates or exact modified-model parameter totals are reported. Repeated and reverse comparisons should not be counted as independent evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss trends over parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from smaller-run power-law fits.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Depth and width variations; a broad range of architectures beyond the tested attention-dimensionality changes.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending of scaling curves.
